candidates.statement: OH CodeActAgent v1.8 + claude-3.5-sonnet reaches a 26.0% resolve rate on SWE-Bench Lite, in the same range as specialist SWE agents (18.0-27.3%).
Swapping the backbone from gpt-4o to claude-3.5-sonnet raises OpenHands' SWE-Bench Lite score from 22.0% to 26.0% with no other change.
OH CodeActAgent v1.5 + gpt-4o fixes 79.3% of HumanEvalFix Python bugs, 0-shot.
candidates.quote: OpenHands CodeActAgent successfully fixes 79.3% of bugs in the Python split

candidates.statement: 79.3% (OpenHands, 0-shot) compares with 48.6% for the best non-agentic baseline (StarCoder2-15B) and 87.7% for SWE-Agent under a 1-shot demonstration.

On WebArena, OpenHands' BrowsingAgent/CodeActAgent (14.5-15.5% with the strongest backbones) is at least as strong as the prior domain-general-prompting baseline (WebArena Agent + gpt-4-turbo, 14.4%), though below specialist trained systems (18.2-20.2%).
On MiniWoB++, OpenHands' best score (40.8%) trails the specialist CC-Net baseline (91.1%) by a wide margin.
On GAIA (L1 validation), OpenHands' GPTSwarm agent (32.1%) more than doubles AutoGPT's score (13.2%).
On GPQA (diamond), OpenHands' CodeActAgent + claude-3.5-sonnet (52.0%) exceeds gpt-4 few-shot chain-of-thought (38.8%) and non-expert humans (21.9%), but remains below expert humans (81.3%).
On AgentBench's OS subset, OpenHands + gpt-4o (57.6%) exceeds the benchmark's own baseline agent + gpt-4 (42.4%).
On MINT, OpenHands + gpt-4o exceeds the MINT baseline agent on the math subset (77.3% vs 65.8%) but trails it on the code subset (50.0% vs 59.6%).
On ProofWriter, OpenHands + gpt-4o (78.8%) is close to but below Logic-LM's neuro-symbolic pipeline (79.6%) and above plain few-shot chain-of-thought (68.1%).
On the Entity Deduction Arena, OpenHands + gpt-4o (38.0%) is roughly level with zero-shot prompting + gpt-4 (40.0%).
The same CodeActAgent, without per-category modification to its system prompt, is competitive across software, web, and miscellaneous-assistance categories.
candidates.quote: the same CodeAct agent, without any modifications to its system prompt, demonstrates competitive performance across three major task categories

candidates.statement: Within the same agent scaffold, benchmark score scales strongly with backbone-LLM capability (e.g. gpt-3.5-turbo-16k 33.8%/5.2% vs gpt-4o 77.3%/50.0% on MINT math/code; gpt-3.5-turbo-0125 11.8% vs gpt-4o 57.6% on AgentBench-OS).
The cross-category competitiveness finding is not uniform: on MiniWoB++ and the MINT code subset OpenHands trails a specialist/baseline system.

No single prior open framework combines a general (not domain-specific) sandboxed code+browser execution runtime, a standardized/extensible tool library, multi-agent delegation, and an integrated evaluation harness in one open platform.
Software is one of the most powerful interfaces available for an agent to act on the world, motivating code execution as OpenHands' core interaction mechanism.
A shared AgentSkills tool library is needed because a carefully crafted agent-computer interface matters, but building/maintaining one bespoke ACI per agent implementation does not scale.

OpenHands chose a code-execution action space (bash/Python/browser) over fixed JSON tool-calling because it is a flexible, reliable, easy-to-maintain set of primitives, while staying compatible with tool-calling agents.
OpenHands isolates every task session in its own Docker sandbox so that agent-driven code execution cannot harm the user's own system.
AgentSkills only adds a tool when the LLM cannot already write the needed code directly, or the tool must call an external model.
OpenHands mocks LLM calls with cached, exact-match prompt/response pairs in its integration-test suite to get deterministic, low-cost regression tests on every pull request.
OpenHands defaults to the SWE-Bench Lite subset and withholds SWE-Bench's optional hint text, for cost-saving and evaluation-realism reasons.
OpenHands is an actively used open-source project: MIT-licensed, 32K GitHub stars, 2.1K+ contributions from 188+ contributors.

The project has continued to expand since publication: an updated SDK, a broader/updated benchmark suite (e.g. SWE-Bench Pro, Commit0, OpenAgentSafety, ProgramBench), and a control-center interface (Agent Canvas) that runs third-party agents (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini) alongside OpenHands' own.
[limitation] Multi-modal file handling (images/video/office documents) is not yet integrated in a principled way.
[limitation, broad/central] Current agents still struggle with complex tasks.
[limitation] The current agent performs poorly when editing long files.
[limitation] The HumanEvalFix comparison against SWE-Agent (87.7%) is 1-shot vs. OpenHands' 0-shot, so it is not a controlled comparison.
[limitation] OpenHands' own agent workflows still require substantial handcrafted engineering; automatic workflow generation is future work.

[writer-derived caveat] Baselines across the 15 benchmarks differ in backbone LLM, shot count, and training regime (prompted vs. fine-tuned vs. RL-trained specialist), so the cross-category pattern is not a controlled, single-variable ablation of the architecture alone.
[writer-derived caveat] No run reports seed/trial variance; single-run point estimates only.
[writer-derived caveat] The competitiveness pattern is not universal: MiniWoB++ and the MINT code subset are counterexamples.
